justifications.functional_suitability: All functional requirements are comprehensively fulfilled. Online submissions are handled via Web Portal (SPA), adjuster operations via Adjuster Portal (SPA), and incremental migration via the Feature Flag / Routing Service and Mainframe Adapter.
justifications.performance_efficiency: The 2s loading requirement is achieved despite 5s mainframe latency by decoupling adjusters using Azure Cosmos DB as a low-latency Claim Read-Model Store and caching views through the Claims API (BFF).
justifications.compatibility: The architecture excels at coexistence: the Mainframe Adapter connects securely via mTLS and ExpressRoute to the Legacy COBOL/DB2 Mainframe, while the Authentication Middleware seamlessly integrates with Active Directory / Azure AD.
justifications.usability: Target user groups receive dedicated frontends: Web Portal (SPA) for Customers and Brokers, Adjuster Portal (SPA) for Claims Adjusters, and Dispute & Exception Dashboard for Operations Managers, all featuring dynamic, reactive forms.
justifications.reliability: Azure Service Bus, Cosmos DB Reconciliation State Store, and Outbound Resilience Policy Engine guarantee consistency and fault tolerance, though explicit handling of the strict nightly batch window constraint is not fully detailed.
justifications.security: Security is addressed thoroughly via Azure AD SSO, Authentication Middleware, HttpOnly cookies, Azure Key Vault with Managed Identities, mTLS over ExpressRoute, and immutable WORM storage in Audit Trail Storage Container.
justifications.maintainability: Feature Flag / Routing Service enables instant claim type rollback within one day. Modularity is well-defined, though deploying Node.js into Azure Kubernetes Service creates maintainability overhead for a team with little cloud experience.
justifications.portability: The hybrid deployment target (on-premise and Azure West Europe) is correctly realized using ExpressRoute and Mainframe Adapter, though components are tightly coupled to proprietary Azure PaaS offerings.

PERF-01.justification: The architecture incorporates a dedicated Claim Read-Model Store in Azure Cosmos DB and caching view-model handlers in the BFF, serving adjuster screens directly without synchronous calls to the legacy mainframe.
sensitivity_points: Cache synchronization latency between the mainframe and Cosmos DB read model
Cosmos DB read throughput and partition key design
tradeoffs: Eventual consistency in adjuster views in exchange for sub-second UI response times

PERF-02.justification: Azure Service Bus topics and queues decouple online submission ingestion from mainframe processing during peak volume. However, explicit scheduling mechanisms to throttle or pause sync traffic during the 23:00-05:00 batch window are not fully specified.
sensitivity_points: Queue depth and buffering capacity in Azure Service Bus under sustained peak
Rate-limiting policies implemented in the Mainframe Adapter
tradeoffs: Asynchronous submission processing delays immediate mainframe confirmation to protect batch windows

AVAIL-01.justification: Online claims are accepted into Azure Service Bus persistent queues while the mainframe is offline. The Mainframe Adapter consumes queued sync messages when the batch window closes, preventing submission loss.
sensitivity_points: Message retention duration and queue quotas in Azure Service Bus
Adapter reconnect and backoff policy after batch window completion
tradeoffs: Queue backlog processing after batch window may increase initial morning sync latency

AVAIL-02.justification: The architecture includes a Reconciliation State Store, Cosmos Change Feed, immutable Audit Trail Storage, and a Dispute & Exception Dashboard for handling synchronization failures, though two-phase distributed state mechanics remain partially abstract.
sensitivity_points: Idempotency token tracking between cloud adapter and legacy DB2 tables
Operational speed of dispute resolution via exception dashboard
tradeoffs: Asynchronous reconciliation requires manual dispute intervention workflows for edge cases

MOD-01.justification: The dedicated Feature Flag / Routing Service (Azure App Configuration) supports atomic rule swaps and circuit breakers. Combined with the Mainframe Adapter, claim types can be rerouted or rolled back instantaneously without code deployment.
sensitivity_points: Cache TTL of feature flags in the BFF and Mainframe Adapter
Mainframe interface schema backward compatibility during rollback
tradeoffs: Runtime routing evaluation overhead against immediate rollback flexibility

MOD-02.justification: Frontends interact solely with the Claims API (BFF) and do not couple to the mainframe. Retiring the mainframe requires updating the BFF routing mediator to persist to Azure data stores and decommissioning the Mainframe Adapter.
sensitivity_points: Strict adherence to API contract isolation between BFF and client SPAs
Data model migration from DB2 schema to target cloud databases
tradeoffs: BFF abstraction layer introduces extra network hop to keep frontend decoupled

SEC-01.justification: The architecture provides authentication middleware, token management, schema validation, and immutable audit logs. However, multi-tenant broker authorization policies and resource-level access control enforcement are not explicitly specified in the components.
sensitivity_points: Enforcement point for broker-to-claim ownership validation
Completeness of security logging on unauthorized access attempts
tradeoffs: Fine-grained data-level access checks increase BFF request processing time

SEC-02.justification: Adjuster access is mediated through Azure AD SSO and token validation middleware in the BFF. Adjusters do not hold direct mainframe accounts. Revocation depends on Azure AD token expiration and session invalidation mechanisms.
sensitivity_points: JWT token lifetime and refresh token revocation latency in Azure AD
Session invalidation policy in Session & Token Manager
tradeoffs: Short-lived access tokens require frequent re-validation, adding slight auth overhead
